# Peripartum Cardiomyopathy: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is a potentially life-threatening form of heart failure that presents toward the end of pregnancy or in the months following delivery, in the absence of another identifiable cause of cardiac dysfunction [1]. The condition is characterized by left ventricular (LV) systolic dysfunction, typically with an ejection fraction (EF) below 45%, and represents an important cause of maternal morbidity and mortality worldwide [2]. The diagnosis remains one of exclusion, requiring careful evaluation to rule out pre-existing cardiomyopathy and other pregnancy-related cardiac complications [3].

## Epidemiology

The incidence of PPCM varies substantially by geographic region and ethnicity. Reported rates range from approximately 1 in 1,000 to 1 in 4,000 live births in the United States, while strikingly higher incidences are observed in Nigeria and Haiti [4,5]. Women of African ancestry appear to be at disproportionately elevated risk [6]. Established risk factors include advanced maternal age, multiparity, multifetal gestation, pre-eclampsia and other hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, and prolonged tocolytic therapy [7,8]. Pre-eclampsia in particular shows a strong epidemiological association, suggesting shared pathophysiological mechanisms [9].

## Pathophysiology

The pathogenesis of PPCM is incompletely understood but is increasingly viewed as a "two-hit" process involving systemic angiogenic imbalance superimposed on individual susceptibility [10]. A leading hypothesis implicates the cleavage of prolactin by cathepsin D into a 16-kDa antiangiogenic fragment that promotes endothelial dysfunction and cardiomyocyte injury [11]. This mechanism provided the rationale for bromocriptine therapy, which suppresses prolactin secretion [12]. Late-gestation antiangiogenic factors, notably soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt-1) secreted by the placenta, contribute to the vascular insult [13]. Oxidative stress and impaired myocardial signaling through the STAT3 pathway have been demonstrated in experimental models [14]. A genetic predisposition is also recognized; truncating variants in *TTN*, encoding the sarcomeric protein titin, are found in a substantial proportion of patients, overlapping with the genetic architecture of dilated cardiomyopathy [15,16].

## Clinical Presentation and Diagnosis

Symptoms of PPCM—dyspnea, fatigue, orthopnea, and peripheral edema—often overlap with those of normal late pregnancy, contributing to delayed diagnosis [17]. Clinicians should maintain a high index of suspicion in peripartum women with persistent or progressive symptoms. Echocardiography is the cornerstone of diagnosis, demonstrating reduced LV systolic function with or without chamber dilatation [18]. Natriuretic peptides (BNP or NT-proBNP) are typically elevated and aid in distinguishing cardiac from physiological causes of dyspnea [19]. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging can provide additional structural information and assist in excluding alternative diagnoses such as myocarditis [20]. The European Society of Cardiology working group has provided consensus diagnostic criteria to standardize identification and research [1].

## Management

Management of PPCM largely follows standard heart failure principles, with modifications for pregnancy and lactation [21]. In women who remain pregnant, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers are contraindicated owing to fetal toxicity, and hydralazine combined with nitrates is preferred [22]. Beta-blockers, particularly beta-1 selective agents, are generally considered safe and beneficial [23]. After delivery, guideline-directed medical therapy including renin-angiotensin system inhibitors, beta-blockers, and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists should be instituted [21]. Because of the prothrombotic state and risk of LV thrombus in severely depressed EF, anticoagulation is often recommended [24]. Bromocriptine, added to standard therapy, has shown promise in improving LV recovery in randomized and registry data, although it requires concomitant anticoagulation [12,25]. For refractory cases, mechanical circulatory support and cardiac transplantation may be necessary [26].

## Prognosis and Future Pregnancies

Outcomes in PPCM are more favorable than in many other cardiomyopathies, with a substantial proportion of women recovering LV function within six to twelve months [27]. However, persistent dysfunction, progression to advanced heart failure, and death occur in a minority [28]. Recovery of myocardial function is the strongest predictor of favorable outcome [29]. Subsequent pregnancies carry a significant risk of relapse, particularly in women who have not recovered normal LV function, and require careful preconception counseling and multidisciplinary monitoring [30].

## Conclusion

PPCM is a distinct and serious cardiomyopathy with multifactorial pathophysiology centered on angiogenic imbalance and genetic susceptibility. Early recognition, prompt initiation of heart failure therapy, and consideration of disease-specific treatments such as bromocriptine can improve outcomes. Continued research into mechanisms and individualized therapy, along with attention to disparities in incidence and access to care, remains essential.
